newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: AKZO'S ELSTERBERG COULD BREAK EVEN IN 1997.
newsitem.headline: AKZO'S ELSTERBERG COULD BREAK EVEN IN 1997.

text.p: Rather than investing 300 million guilders in a new plant, Dutch chemicals giant Akzo Nobel chose to snap up a loss-making viscose factory from East Germany's privatisation agency Treuhand for less than half that in the early 1990s.
Five years on, the Elsterberg Werk textiles plant is still in the red, but hopes to make its first operating profit in 1997 on annual sales of around 75 million marks.
"If we do our utmost, and everything goes all right, we could break even next year," said Moritz Gimpel, Akzo's viscose production manager said during a tour around the site.

Akzo and Treuhandsanstalt have invested 160 million marks to date in new assets for the completely depleted plant, which makes an annual 5,000 tonnes of viscose. Eastern European countries have recently unleashed a viscose price war.
Akzo is tight-lipped over the amount of money it pumped into Elsterberg and how much came from Treuhand, but large subsidies were an inherent part of the East German privatisation company.

Akzo produces viscose textile at four other locations, three in Germany and one in the Netherlands, but it has recently begun preparations to transfer labour-intensive viscose processing activities from these sites to the Polish city of Gorzow.

So far, Elsterberg has escaped from such plans as labour costs are around 65 percent of those in West Germany, but the processing jobs there would also be at risk if wages continued to rise, said Akzo's board member Friedrich Froehlich.
"If we are able to agree a long-term wage contract with the unions, we could keep all jobs here in Elsterberg," he said.

Elsterberg, which has 460 staff, may even be in the running to become the production site for a viscose-related fibre called Newcell that Akzo is developing with Britain's Courtaulds on the basis of that firm's lyocel cellulose fibre.
But Froehlich said wages in Britain were similar to those in East Germany and location in the U.K. was also possible.
"We keep our options open. We haven't taken a decision yet," he said.
Meanwhile, the German state of Saxony has rallied to lure foreign investment to its region in an attempt to cut jobless rates from the current 15-20 percent of the workforce.
But Froehlich said Akzo had not yet talked subsidies with Saxony's prime minister Kurt Biedenkopf, who was guest of honour at an Akzo presentation in Dresden.

Biedenkopf was in the news earlier this week after European Competition Commissioner Karel van Miert approved "illegal aid" from Saxony to Volkswagen AG for construction of a greenfield plant, but blocking the same amount of German federal subsidies.

Akzo bought Elsterberg in 1991 because of its location in the heart of a textiles region and also because rivals were eying the plant. Before Communist nationalisation in 1949, the site belonged to Vereinigten Glanzstoff-fabriken, which was later taken over by Akzo.
After German reunification, the Saxon textiles manufacturing industry has largely collapsed.
